--- title: "Regression performance measures" description: "RMSE, MAE and R² each weigh errors their own way, and on skewed counts they can choose different models: MAE picks a forest that predicts only about two thirds of the animals caught." order: 3 categories: [validation, metrics, regression] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Measures can rank the same models differently Most pages so far have scored models by the RMSE, with R² beside it now and then. Both are **performance measures**: numbers that sum up how far a model's predictions fall from the observed values. Each measure weighs the errors its own way, so two measures can rank the same models differently, and a model can win on one by being wrong in a way the other ignores. This page sets the common measures side by side and shows why they part on skewed counts. Which one to report depends on what the predictions are for, which [Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) sets out. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Three measures weigh errors differently A prediction's error is the observed value minus the prediction, the [residual](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) of one station. Each measure below turns the errors of many stations into one number. | Measure | What it is | What it minds most | | --- | --- | --- | | **RMSE** | the square root of the average squared error | large errors | | **MAE**, the mean absolute error | the average size of an error, its sign dropped | every unit of error the same | | **R²** | one minus the squared errors over the squared spread of the observed values around their average | the same errors as the RMSE, compared with predicting the average | [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd#rmse-measures-a-typical-miss-on-the-test-stations) built the RMSE by hand, and MAE is the absolute error of [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd), used here to score rather than to fit. A forest fitted with squared error can be scored by MAE. For the RMSE and MAE, lower is better. R² is 1 for perfect predictions, 0 for predictions no better than the average of the observed values, and below 0 for worse. Each measure is at its best at a different prediction, as each loss is in [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#each-loss-aims-at-a-different-middle-of-the-data): the RMSE and R² when a model predicts the average of the values it could observe, MAE when it predicts the median. For counts with a long right tail the median sits below the average, so MAE favours models that predict low. ## Software often reports the squared correlation as R² This course reports the R² in the table above: `rsq_trad()` in yardstick and `r2_score()` in scikit-learn. Many programs and papers report something else under the same name: the **squared correlation** between the observed and predicted values, which is yardstick's `rsq()`. It asks only whether the predictions rise and fall with the observed values, so predictions that are all too low by the same proportion keep a perfect score. When a paper reports R², check which one it means. ::: {.diagram} ![Two definitions of R². Left, predictions in the right pattern but too low: the squared correlation is perfect, and R² is low because it counts the gap to the line where the predicted value equals the observed one. Right, predictions at the right level with scatter: both measures agree. The two definitions rank the two sets of predictions in opposite orders.](img/two-r-squared.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each a scatter of eight predicted values against observed values, with a dashed line where predicted equals observed. Left, right pattern, too low: the points lie on a straight line of half the slope, below the dashed line; squared correlation 1.00, R² 0.17. Right, right level, scattered: the points sit above and below the dashed line; squared correlation 0.73, R² 0.70. A note says squared correlation asks how closely the points follow some straight line, whatever its slope, and R² asks how close they come to the dashed line: one minus the squared misses, divided by the squared spread of the observed values around their average."} ::: ## Worked example Four models predict the survey's counts: - **Predicting the average**: every station gets the average count of the fitted stations. It has no skill, and the other three should beat it. - **Linear regression**, from [Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd), the simple baseline. - **Random forest**, from [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). - **Random forest on log counts**, the same forest fitted to the log of the count plus 1, each prediction turned back into animals, as in [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#training-on-log-counts-predicts-far-fewer-animals-than-were-caught). Every model is cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked out from the pooled out-of-fold predictions, as on [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd). Every measure therefore scores the same predictions of the same stations. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |> mutate(log_abundance = log1p(abundance)) set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") with_inputs <- function(outcome, model) { recipe(reformulate(inputs, outcome), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> workflow(model) } forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression") average <- null_model(mode = "regression") log_forest <- "Random forest on log counts" models <- list( "Predicting the average" = with_inputs("abundance", average), "Linear regression" = with_inputs("abundance", linear_reg()), "Random forest" = with_inputs("abundance", forest), "Random forest on log counts" = with_inputs("log_abundance", forest) ) # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) { fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) }) # back from log counts to animals out_of_fold[[log_forest]] <- expm1(out_of_fold[[log_forest]]) predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |> mutate(caught = survey$abundance) |> pivot_longer(-caught, names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted") |> mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) tibble(stations = nrow(survey), `average catch` = round(mean(survey$abundance), 2), `median catch` = median(survey$abundance), `stations with none` = mean(survey$abundance == 0)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| average catch| median catch| stations with none| |--------:|-------------:|------------:|------------------:| | 800| 3.9| 2| 0.225|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score, root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() caught = survey["abundance"] folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical] def with_inputs(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) # max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does. forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1) models = { "Predicting the average": DummyRegressor(), "Linear regression": LinearRegression(), "Random forest": forest, # fitted to log counts, each prediction turned back into animals "Random forest on log counts": TransformedTargetRegressor( forest, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1), } # every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"]) for name, model in models.items()} predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(caught=caught) .melt(id_vars="caught", var_name="model", value_name="predicted")) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "average catch": [round(caught.mean(), 2)], "median catch": [caught.median()], "stations with none": [(caught == 0).mean()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | average catch | median catch | stations with none | |-----------:|----------------:|---------------:|---------------------:| | 800 | 3.9 | 2 | 0.225 | ::: ::: ::: The counts are skewed: the average station caught 3.90 animals, the median station 2, and 22% of the stations caught none. ### RMSE and MAE choose different forests The last column adds up each model's predictions over all the stations and divides by the number of animals caught: 1 means the model predicts the right total. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scores <- predictions |> summarise(RMSE = rmse_vec(caught, predicted), MAE = mae_vec(caught, predicted), `R²` = rsq_trad_vec(caught, predicted), `predicted / caught` = sum(predicted) / sum(caught), .by = model) scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | RMSE| MAE| R²| predicted / caught| |:---------------------------|----:|----:|----:|------------------:| |Predicting the average | 4.78| 3.39| 0.00| 1.00| |Linear regression | 4.39| 3.11| 0.15| 1.00| |Random forest | 4.32| 2.95| 0.18| 1.04| |Random forest on log counts | 4.47| 2.76| 0.12| 0.69|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} scores = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(g.caught, g.predicted), "MAE": mean_absolute_error(g.caught, g.predicted), "R²": r2_score(g.caught, g.predicted), "predicted / caught": g.predicted.sum() / g.caught.sum(), }), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) scores.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | RMSE | MAE | R² | predicted / caught | |:----------------------------|-------:|------:|------:|---------------------:| | Predicting the average | 4.78 | 3.39 | -0 | 1 | | Linear regression | 4.39 | 3.1 | 0.15 | 0.99 | | Random forest | 4.25 | 2.89 | 0.21 | 0.99 | | Random forest on log counts | 4.5 | 2.78 | 0.11 | 0.66 | ::: ::: ::: The RMSE picks the random forest, at 4.32. MAE picks the random forest on log counts, at 2.76, a model that comes third of four on the RMSE, behind linear regression and the random forest. R² counts the same squared errors as the RMSE, so it ranks the models in the same order, with predicting the average at about zero. The last column shows why. The forest on log counts predicts 69% of the animals caught; the other models predict close to all of them. Fitted to log counts, it aims near the median catch, below the average, as [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#training-on-log-counts-predicts-far-fewer-animals-than-were-caught) found, and MAE, smallest at the median, rewards exactly that. For a stock estimate or a map total, MAE has picked the model that misses 31% of the animals. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Performance measures** weigh errors differently. The **RMSE** and R² are at their best when a model predicts the average of what could be observed, **MAE** when it predicts the median. - On these skewed counts the RMSE picked the random forest and MAE the random forest on log counts, which predicts only 69% of the animals caught. - The **squared correlation**, which much software reports as R², cannot see predictions that are too low across the board. The R² used here, `rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()`, can. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Multiply the forest on log counts' predictions by one number, chosen so that their total matches the catch of the fitted stations in each fold. Predict first: which model does MAE pick now? 2. Add the squared correlation, `rsq_vec()`, to the table. Predict first: does the forest on log counts score as well on it as the plain forest?
